title: A failing readiness probe takes a Pod out of rotation without restarting it
dek: A short Japanese talk, translated here, separates two Kubernetes probes by what happens when they fail. Its terminal shows the readiness half.

sections.heading: Two probes, two different responses to failure

blocks.text: The speaker sets out to explain how readiness and liveness probes differ [@j-intro]. The answer, in translation, is about consequences. A failing readiness probe removes the Pod from the Service's endpoints but does not restart it [@j-ready]:
readinessプローブが失敗すると、Podはサービスのエンドポイントから外されますが、再起動はされません。

A failing liveness probe is different: the kubelet restarts the container [@j-live]. The Kubernetes documentation says the same. A failed readiness probe removes the Pod's IP address from the EndpointSlices of matching Services, while repeated liveness failures make the kubelet restart the container [@k8s].

sections.heading: The terminal shows a Pod that is running, not ready, and never restarted

blocks.text: On screen, the configuration sets a readiness probe on `/ready` every five seconds and a liveness probe on `/healthz` with a failure threshold of three [@j-config]. The Pod listing then shows `READY 0/1`, `STATUS Running`, and `RESTARTS 0` [@j-pods].
That is what a failing readiness probe looks like: out of rotation, still running, not restarted. The video does not say which probe failed, so this reading is ours.

sections.heading: Slow starters get a third probe

blocks.text: For slow-starting apps, the speaker calls a startup probe 定石 (*joseki*), translated here as the standard move [@j-startup]. The word comes from the game of Go, where it names an established sequence of play. It is stronger than a habit and weaker than a rule, so we keep the original term.
The documentation agrees that startup probes suit containers that take a long time to come into service, and that liveness and readiness checks wait until the startup probe succeeds [@k8s].

sections.heading: The timeout the speaker chose is not recoverable

blocks.text: The speaker says they set a timeout, but the number is inaudible and never appears on screen [@j-timeout]. We do not guess it.

brief.question: What happens to a Pod when each probe fails?

evidence.text: The speaker says a failing readiness probe removes the Pod from Service endpoints without a restart, and a failing liveness probe restarts the container.
The Pod listing shows READY 0/1, STATUS Running, RESTARTS 0.
Kubernetes documents the same failure responses and recommends startup probes for slow starters.
Slow-starting apps should use a startup probe (the speaker's 定石).
The timeout value the speaker set is inaudible and not shown.

proposals.text: Use readiness for warm-up and dependency checks, and keep liveness for states a restart actually fixes, such as deadlock.
proposals.risks: A liveness probe that checks dependencies can restart healthy containers under load.

proposals.text: Recover the timeout from the speaker's slides or repository before reusing the configuration.

limitations: The English is a translation of Japanese speech, not the speaker's words; 定石 is kept in the original because its translation is lossy.
Evaluation fixture: generated slides and a tone for audio, so this article does not test transcription or translation accuracy.
The timeout value is unknown, and the video does not show which probe failed.
